title: Don’t You Dare Forget These Truths about Teaching
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Prompted by reader comments on an earlier post comparing Common Core literacy skills to Bill Coplin's list of what employers want, Stuart pauses to state two truths he says must frame any conversation about standards. The first is that no single teacher can make a child develop these skills: parents, other teachers and administrators, and the child are co-laborers, and imagining oneself a lone warrior is quixotic rather than heroic. He is careful not to turn this into an excuse, calling it a license to rest after a solid day's work, not a license to stop improving, and insisting a teacher's job is to teach and grow rather than single-handedly produce test scores. The second truth is that focus drives impact: schools fail not because teachers slack but because they work too hard on too many things, so the Common Core will succeed only if teachers are allowed to work on a few standards at a time. He points administrators to Mike Schmoker's Focus as the case for a short list. The remainder clarifies that Coplin's book targets college students yet still serves high schoolers, because success requires strategic rather than merely hard work.
points: Stuart's first truth reframes accountability: parents, colleagues, administrators and the student himself share responsibility for skill growth, so a lone-teacher mindset is quixotic, not heroic.
He draws a careful line between rest and complacency, calling shared responsibility a blank check to take a break after solid work but never to stop improving as an instructor and motivator.
His diagnosis of struggling schools inverts the usual complaint: the problem is not teachers mailing it in but teachers working too hard on too many priorities.
The Common Core's success, he predicts, depends on teachers being given permission - even a directive - to work on only a few standards at a time, with Schmoker's Focus as the supporting text.
He uses Coplin's employer-skills book with high schoolers to teach that successful people are strategic about their work, not merely hardworking.
quotes: I strongly believe in the power of our calling as educators, but we cannot allow ourselves to freak out when we read lists like the one I compiled in my last post.

Look: the list above isn't a list of scapegoats; it is a list of co-laborers in the quest for a kid to live a fulfilling life. That's common sense; if any of us fancies ourselves a lone warrior in the battle for a kid's life, we're not being heroic–we're being quixotic.
I'm just saying that I'm definitely not God, and you probably aren't either. We do our best each day, we try to constantly improve, and we go home and sleep well.

This isn't a blank check for you to stop working on your abilities as an instructor and, yes, as a motivator; it is a blank check to give yourself a break after a solid day of work. Your job is to teach and grow; it's not to single-handedly produce test scores.

The problem with most schools isn't that teachers aren't working hard enough — in fact, I've never found a school where anywhere close to the majority of teachers are mailing it in. The problem is actually the opposite: teachers are working too freaking hard on way too many things.

If your administrators don't give you this kind of empowering permission (or if they forget that they gave it to you as soon as they attend the latest educonference), gift them with a common sense book like Mike Schmoker's Focus. You may not agree with everything he says, but his underlying premise is solid.
